ety.text: From Middle English acre, aker, from Old English æcer (“field where crops are grown”), from Proto-West Germanic *akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”). Doublet of agriculture.

senses.d: An English unit of land area (symbol: a. or ac.) originally denoting a day's ploughing for a yoke of oxen, now standardized as 4,840 square yards or 4,046.86 square metres.
An area of 10,240 square yards or 4 quarters.
Any of various similar units of area in other systems.
A wide expanse.
ex: I like my new house—there’s acres of space!

senses.d: A large quantity.
A field.
The acre's breadth by the length, English units of length equal to the statute dimensions of the acre: 22 yd (≈20 m) by 220 yd (≈200 m).
A duel fought between individual Scots and Englishmen in the borderlands.

ety.text: Anglo-Norman an croizbor. Middle English acros English across From Middle English acros, from early Middle English a-croiz, a-creoyz, from Anglo-Norman an (“in, on”) + croiz (“in the form of a cross”). More at cross. By surface analysis, a- + cross.

senses.d: To, toward, or from the far side of (something that lies between two points of interest).
ex: Fortunately, there was a bridge across the river.

senses.d: On the opposite side of (something that lies between two points of interest).
ex: That store is across the street.

senses.d: across from: on the opposite side, relative to something that lies between, from (a point of interest).
ex: And make sure you're parked across the mall in the outside lot. […] Last time I was there, I parked in a parking structure and paid an arm and a leg for it.
A boy that sat across me politely introduced himself as Jackson Klausner.

senses.d: From one side to the other within (a space being traversed).
ex: The meteor streaked across the sky.

senses.d: At or near the far end of (a space).
Spanning.
ex: This poetry speaks across the centuries.

senses.d: Throughout.
ex: All across the country, voters were communicating their representatives.

senses.d: So as to intersect or pass through or over at an angle.
ex: Lay the top stick across the bottom one.
She had straps fastened across the conduit every six feet.

senses.d: In possession of full, up-to-date information about; abreast of.
ex: Keep across all the latest news here at Channel 10.
As a regular news reader I thought I was across the eccentricities of the US president.

senses.d: From one side to the other.
ex: she helped the blind man across; the river is half a mile across

senses.d: On the other side.
ex: If we sail off at noon, when will we be across?

senses.d: In a particular direction.
ex: He leaned across for a book.

senses.d: Horizontally.
